claims.text: First labs: CBC, ESR or CRP, urinalysis, and a pregnancy test when indicated.
claims.quote: Initial laboratory tests should include a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein, a pregnancy test, if indicated, and urinalysis.

claims.text: Other labs as the picture suggests: liver function tests, amylase and/or lipase, STI testing, and stool studies including occult blood.
claims.quote: Other tests may include liver function tests; amylase, lipase, or both for pancreatitis; sexually transmitted infection testing (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae); and stool studies (Escherichia coli and Campylobacter, Cryptosporidium, Salmonella, and Shigella species), including evaluation for occult blood.

claims.text: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging for undifferentiated acute abdominal pain in children, and uses no radiation.
claims.quote: Ultrasonography is relatively inexpensive and does not expose the patient to radiation. It is the first-line imaging choice for undifferentiated acute abdominal pain, unless history or physical examination identifies a specific diagnosis.

claims.text: Suspected appendicitis: ultrasound first, then CT or MRI if it is equivocal.
claims.quote: Ultrasonography is the imaging tool of choice for evaluation of appendicitis, followed by CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for equivocal findings.

claims.text: Abdominal X-ray can show a stone, a mass, an ingested foreign body, free air from perforation, or constipation.
claims.quote: Radiography may identify a renal or ureteric calculus, abdominal mass, ingested foreign body (including bezoars), bowel perforation with free air, and constipation.

claims.text: WBC is often 12,000 to 15,000/mcL in appendicitis, but a normal count does not exclude it.
claims.quote: Laboratory studies typically show leukocytosis (12,000 to 15,000/mcL [12.00 to 15.00 × 10 9 /L]), but this finding is highly variable; a normal white blood cell count should not be used to exclude appendicitis.
